Origins and Evolution of Cult of the Dead Cow

Members of the Cult of the Dead Cow (cDc) reflect on the transition from 1980s bulletin board system (BBS) culture and cyberpunk aesthetics to early DEF CON gatherings. Early hacker conventions prioritized informal social networking and underground knowledge sharing over structured conference tracks.

Hacker Conventions as Performance and Spectacle

The cDc approached their DEF CON appearances not merely as technical podium lectures, but as immersive multimedia rock shows. Bringing custom sound reinforcement gear, stage lighting, and provocative visual media, the group turned technical disclosures into high-energy theatrical events that defined convention lore.

Handling Mainstream Press and Media Circuses

Rather than avoiding mainstream media scrutiny, cDc actively engaged with journalists and television networks to influence public perception of hacker culture. Group members recount elaborate pranks played on visiting media crews and corporate observers, including staging satirical press conferences and demand letters.

Maturation of the Information Security Industry

The reflections capture a pivotal shift as hacker conventions evolved from chaotic countercultural gatherings into vital networking hubs and career launchpads. Despite commercialization and professionalization across the security industry, the core ethos of creative mischief and community solidarity persisted.

talks.summary:
Transitioning from Penetration Testing to Humanitarian Aid

Johnny Long describes his career pivot after fifteen years in professional penetration testing, authoring security books, and speaking at major hacker conferences. Seeking greater purpose beyond technical testing, an eye-opening trip to Uganda revealed the critical impact basic computer support could have on vulnerable populations.

Founding Hackers for Charity

Recognizing that international aid organizations and local charities frequently struggle with malfunctioning computing equipment, Long established Hackers for Charity (HFC). The initiative mobilized technologists to clean malware-infected computers, restore financial systems, and secure IT operations for non-profits operating in East Africa.

Fundraising and Community Support at DEF CON

DEF CON served as a foundational support network for Hackers for Charity, providing booth space to sell merchandise, handcrafted goods from Ugandan artisans, and host annual benefit auctions. Prominent community members and security companies regularly contributed rare conference badges and equipment to fund charitable operations.

Challenging Stereotypes of Hacker Culture

The work of Hackers for Charity directly countered persistent public stereotypes of hackers as purely malicious actors. By demonstrating that technical problem-solving skills could build communication networks during disasters and support humanitarian logistics, the initiative highlighted the philanthropic spirit of the hacker community.

talks.title: Documentary Bonus Clips - Not the Same Anymore
talks.teaser: Documentary Bonus Clips - Not the Same Anymore — DEF CON Conference upload.
talks.summary:
End of an Era at DEF CON 20

A veteran attendee reflects on the bittersweet cultural evolution marking DEF CON's twentieth anniversary. As attendees aged and the cybersecurity profession formalized, early conversations focused purely on shellcode and underground exploits gave way to discussions about career demands, family, and physical stamina.

The Challenge of Informal Social Spaces

During DEF CON's tenure at the Alexis Park hotel, every villa room was an open party welcoming all attendees. As attendance surged into the thousands, access to evening parties required formal invitations and badge lines, altering the spontaneous, egalitarian social environment that characterized early conferences.

Scaling Security Culture and Human Connections

The speaker examines the fundamental tension between rapid community growth and inclusive culture. When a gathering grows too large, maintaining personal friendships and welcoming newcomers becomes logistically difficult, demanding conscious effort to preserve shared values and traditions.

Optimism for Community Resilience

Despite the inevitable pressures of industry commercialization and institutionalization, the narrative concludes on an optimistic note. The speaker emphasizes an enduring commitment to fixing technological vulnerabilities and sustaining the unique camaraderie, passion, and spirit of the hacker community.

talks.title: Documentary Bonus Clips - The Organization
talks.teaser: Documentary Bonus Clips - The Organization — DEF CON Conference upload.
talks.summary:
From Informal Coordination to Structured Operations

A veteran Goon leader details the operational metamorphosis of DEF CON from DEF CON 7 to DEF CON 20. Early conventions relied on small groups making ad-hoc decisions based strictly on seniority, whereas modern editions require a sophisticated management structure to handle tens of thousands of participants safely.

Key Roles in Conference Logistics

The administrative hierarchy coordinates specialized teams to ensure smooth operations across the venue. Central figures include founder Jeff Moss, lead events coordinator Cheryl managing hotel contracts and logistics, and head Goon Zach directing convention security teams alongside specialized department leads.

Managing Contests and Events Operations

The Contests and Events division represents roughly one-third of the total conference footprint. Overseeing dozens of complex, simultaneous challenges requires a dedicated staff of dozens of specialized Goons, with operational rosters expanding continuously to meet attendee demand.

The Paradox of Professionalization

The speaker candidly reflects on the personal contrast between his 18-year-old punk rock hacker self and his current role as a suburban corporate professional with a formal organizational chart. While formal hierarchy might provoke ironic amusement from early countercultural attendees, it represents the essential infrastructure required to keep DEF CON viable.

talks.title: Documentary Bonus Clips - We Make No Money From You
talks.teaser: Documentary Bonus Clips - We Make No Money From You — DEF CON Conference upload.
talks.summary:
Friction with Venue Management at Alexis Park

DEF CON founder Jeff Moss recalls contentious interactions with hotel management during the convention's historic tenure at the Alexis Park Resort. Frequent turnover in hotel executive leadership created recurring tension, with each new general manager questioning why an unorthodox hacker convention was permitted on the property.

The Disconnect Over Event Profitability

During a pre-conference meeting prior to DEF CON's final year at the hotel, the resort CEO claimed the event was financially unprofitable despite attendees completely booking every room and exhausting food and beverage supplies. Conference organizers were baffled by assertions that maximum property occupancy resulted in net financial losses.

Uncovering Internal Hotel Embezzlement

An investigation subsequently revealed that the perceived financial deficit had nothing to do with DEF CON attendees. The hotel's chief financial officer was actively embezzling funds, while staff members were raiding cold storage lockers, stealing alcoholic inventory, and falsifying accounting records by attributing losses to the conference.

External Perception and Institutional Bias

The incident illustrates how unconventional groups can be unfairly scapegoated for internal organizational failures. Even when convention organizers acted entirely in good faith and drove unprecedented business volume, ingrained external biases led property owners to assume hacker malfeasance before uncovering internal crime.

Discovering the Bed Jumping Mafia

Jeff Moss recounts discovering the existence of the Bed Jumping Mafia, a spontaneous, uncoordinated convention subculture operating at the Alexis Park during early DEF CON gatherings. Learning about the phenomenon from a conversation at a Seattle coffee shop highlighted how organic attendee traditions flourish independently of conference planning.

Late Night Room Visits and Pajama Raids

The tradition originated around DEF CON 7 as a playful group of female attendees dressed in pajamas who visited friends' hotel rooms late at night simply to bounce enthusiastically on the beds. The visits were lighthearted and friendly, designed as whimsical social disruptions rather than destructive pranks.

The Legend and Reality of Broken Beds

While rumors circulated that the troupe deliberately broke hotel furniture, Moss clarifies that structural bed failures were rare, accidental consequences of exuberant group jumping rather than malicious intent. Nonetheless, explaining broken mattresses to baffled hotel staff became an entertaining piece of DEF CON mythology.

Organic Traditions in Hacker Culture

The Bed Jumping Mafia exemplifies the grassroots, decentralized culture that defines DEF CON. The most memorable convention memories often emerge organically from attendee creativity and playful camaraderie rather than official conference programming.

Early DEF CON Desert Expeditions

A veteran hacker recounts meeting Sir Dystic (future creator of Back Orifice) for the first time alongside Aleph One (Phrack editor) and White Knight during early DEF CON gatherings in the 1990s.

Mischief in the Nevada Desert

The group headed out into the desert surrounding Las Vegas with shotguns and fireworks, engaging in an anarchic, Hunter S. Thompson-style outing that became a defining personal memory of early hacker culture.
